key_points.point: Randomize at the user/account level, not the session or pageview level.
Bucketing must be sticky: the same user always sees the same variant across sessions.
Session-level randomization causes carryover/contamination when users see both variants.

drill_questions.question: You are testing a redesigned checkout button. An engineer proposes randomizing by pageview because it is trivial to implement. What is wrong with that, and what should the randomization unit be?

rubric.check: Randomization unit is the entity the treatment is applied to and measured on.
Bucketing is sticky so a user never sees both variants.
Names the bias that session-level randomization introduces.

scenarios.sample_answer: Randomize at the user (or account) level, not the pageview level. Pageview randomization means the same user sees both variants across sessions, which causes carryover and muddies the treatment effect. Use sticky bucketing (e.g. hash of user id) so every session for a user lands in the same variant for the whole experiment.
scenarios.scenario: Your team wants to A/B test a redesigned checkout button. An engineer proposes randomizing by pageview because it is the easiest to implement in the existing logging.
scenarios.title: Randomization unit: user vs session

key_points.point: Pick one primary metric before launch; decide the ship/no-ship rule from it.
Guardrail metrics (error rate, latency, crash rate) must not regress; they can veto a launch.
Secondary/diagnostic metrics explain movement but do not decide the launch.

drill_questions.question: The team wants to test a faster ranking model. Name one primary metric, two guardrail metrics, and explain what happens if the primary metric wins but a guardrail regresses.

rubric.check: Exactly one primary metric is chosen before the experiment starts.
Guardrails cover quality/reliability and can block a launch.
Clear decision rule for conflicting metric movements.

scenarios.sample_answer: Primary: conversion rate (or revenue per user) — the metric the business cares about. Guardrails: p99 latency and error/crash rate, plus maybe support-ticket rate. If the primary wins but a guardrail regresses, you do not ship: guardrails are invariants. Investigate, fix the regression, and re-test.
scenarios.scenario: The ranking team built a faster model and wants to A/B test it. Product asks: 'what metrics do we look at?' Someone suggests watching 'all the dashboards' and deciding after.
scenarios.title: Guardrail metrics

key_points.point: Peeking inflates the Type I error rate: repeated looks at p<0.05 produce false positives far more often than 5%.
Pre-commit to a fixed horizon / sample size computed from a power analysis.
If you must peek, use sequential methods: alpha spending, group-sequential designs, or always-valid p-values.

drill_questions.question: A PM checks the experiment dashboard every morning and plans to ship as soon as p < 0.05. Explain why this is a problem and give two concrete fixes.

rubric.check: Explains that repeated significance checks inflate the false-positive rate.
Fix 1: fixed horizon / pre-committed sample size.
Fix 2: a valid sequential method, or CUPED/variance reduction to reach the horizon faster.

scenarios.sample_answer: Peeking is optional stopping: if you test at p<0.05 every day for 20 days, the chance of at least one false positive is far above 5% (roughly 1-(0.95)^20 under independence). Fixes: (1) pre-commit to a fixed horizon from a power calculation and only decide at the end; (2) use sequential methods (alpha spending, group-sequential, always-valid p-values) if interim looks are required. CUPED can also shrink the needed runtime.
scenarios.scenario: A PM checks the experiment dashboard every morning and announces: 'we will ship as soon as the result is significant at p < 0.05.'
scenarios.title: The peeking problem

key_points.point: The lift may be a novelty effect that decays as users habituate.
Run long enough to observe the steady state, not just the launch bump.
Segment by new vs existing users, or compare early vs late periods, to diagnose novelty.

drill_questions.question: The new homepage layout shows +8% engagement in week 1, decaying to +2% by week 4. How do you interpret this, and what would you do before shipping?

rubric.check: Identifies the decaying lift as a likely novelty effect.
Decision is based on the steady-state effect, not the launch bump.
Proposes a diagnostic: new vs existing users, or early vs late window.

scenarios.sample_answer: This smells like a novelty effect: users engage more with anything new, then habituate. Do not ship on the week-1 number. Run until the effect stabilizes and judge the steady-state lift; segment new vs existing users (existing users show novelty more) and compare the first vs last week of the run to confirm the decay.
scenarios.scenario: A redesigned homepage shows +8% engagement in week 1 of the test, but the lift decays to +2% by week 4.
scenarios.title: Novelty effects

key_points.point: This violates SUTVA: one user's outcome depends on other users' treatment assignments.
Randomize at the level of independent clusters (network clusters or geos), not individual users.
Alternative: switchback (time-split) designs when clustering is impractical.

drill_questions.question: You are testing a referral bonus: treated users invite friends, and invited friends may be in the control group. What assumption is violated, and how do you redesign the experiment?

rubric.check: Names the SUTVA / no-interference violation (spillover between units).
Proposes cluster randomization at an independent unit.
Mentions a fallback design (switchback) or acknowledges the trade-off in power.

scenarios.sample_answer: This violates SUTVA — the no-interference assumption: a control user's outcome depends on whether their friends were treated. Redesign with cluster randomization: randomize whole network clusters (or geos) so interference stays inside the cluster. If clusters are impractical, use a switchback design that alternates treatment over time periods.
scenarios.scenario: You are testing a referral bonus feature. Treated users invite their friends, and those friends — who may be assigned to control — change their behavior because of the invitation.
scenarios.title: Network interference

key_points.point: Run a chi-square goodness-of-fit test of observed vs expected split.
SRM usually means broken randomization, a logging bug, or post-assignment filtering (e.g. analyzing only triggered users).
Do not trust the result; diagnose and fix before reading any treatment effect.

drill_questions.question: A 50/50 experiment shows a 52/48 split after a week. Walk through exactly what you check and what you conclude.

rubric.check: Runs a statistical SRM check (chi-square), not eyeballing.
Lists likely root causes: randomization bug, logging, post-assignment filtering.
Does not interpret the treatment effect until SRM is resolved.

scenarios.sample_answer: First run a chi-square goodness-of-fit test against the expected 50/50; with enough traffic 52/48 is significant. SRM almost always means something is broken: a randomization/bucketing bug, telemetry loss correlated with variant, or analyzing only 'triggered' users where triggering itself differs by variant. Do not read the treatment effect — diagnose the pipeline, fix it, and restart.
scenarios.scenario: A 50/50 A/B test shows a 52/48 split after one week of traffic. The PM says 'close enough, let us read the results.'
scenarios.title: Sample ratio mismatch

key_points.point: Commit to a single primary metric before launch.
The primary metric should ladder up to the business goal, not just be easy to move.
It must be sensitive enough to move within the experiment's runtime.

drill_questions.question: The team proposes optimizing click-through rate for a checkout experiment. Argue for or against, and state what you would pick as the primary metric instead if needed.

rubric.check: Exactly one pre-committed primary metric.
Primary metric connects to the business goal (not a vanity proxy).
Considers sensitivity / measurability trade-off.

scenarios.sample_answer: CTR is a weak proxy here: clicks do not pay the bills, and it is gameable (clickbait layouts). Pick one primary metric tied to the goal — e.g. conversion rate or revenue per visitor — committed before launch. Keep CTR as a diagnostic to explain movement, not to decide the ship.
scenarios.scenario: For a checkout-flow experiment the team proposes click-through rate as the success metric because 'it moves fast and we can read it in days.'
scenarios.title: Choosing the primary metric

key_points.point: Compute the required runtime from a power analysis on the minimum meaningful effect.
Cover at least one full weekly cycle (ideally two) to average out day-of-week effects.
Size for the minimum practically meaningful effect, not the smallest detectable one.

drill_questions.question: How long should this experiment run? Give the concrete inputs you need and the non-statistical constraint you would still enforce.

rubric.check: Runtime comes from a power/sample-size calculation on an MDE.
Covers full business cycles (weekly seasonality).
Distinguishes statistical detectability from practical meaningfulness.

scenarios.sample_answer: Inputs: baseline rate, the minimum effect that would actually change the decision (MDE), alpha, and power; that gives required sample size, which divided by daily traffic gives days. Then round up to cover at least one or two full weekly cycles so weekday/weekend mix is representative. Never stop early on a peek.
scenarios.scenario: 'How long do we need to run this?' The baseline conversion rate is 10%, daily traffic is 50k users per variant, and the team will only ship for a lift of at least 1 percentage point.
scenarios.title: How long to run

key_points.point: Testing many metrics/variants inflates the chance of at least one false positive.
Apply a correction: Bonferroni/Holm for family-wise control, or Benjamini-Hochberg for FDR.
Pre-register one primary metric; treat the rest as exploratory.

drill_questions.question: The team tests 4 variants against control on 5 metrics each and ships the one cell with p = 0.03. What is wrong and how do you fix the analysis?

rubric.check: Identifies the multiple-comparisons / winner's-curse problem.
Proposes a concrete correction (Bonferroni/Holm/FDR).
Pre-registers a primary metric/variant comparison.

scenarios.sample_answer: With 4x5 = 20 comparisons, you expect about one p < 0.05 by chance alone — this is p-hacking by design. Pre-register one primary comparison, and correct the rest: Bonferroni or Holm for strict family-wise control, Benjamini-Hochberg if you can tolerate a false discovery rate. The 'winning' cell needs to survive the correction.
scenarios.scenario: The team tests 4 variants against control, looks at 5 metrics each, and ships the single variant-metric cell with p = 0.03.
scenarios.title: Multiple comparisons

key_points.point: A non-significant result is not evidence of no effect — absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
Check the confidence interval and whether the test was powered for the MDE.
Decide: ship if CI rules out meaningful harm, iterate if underpowered, kill if the idea is exhausted.

drill_questions.question: The experiment ends flat: +0.2% with p = 0.45. The team says 'the feature does nothing, kill it.' How do you respond?

rubric.check: Does not equate non-significance with zero effect.
Uses the confidence interval / power to bound what effects are ruled out.
Gives a decision framework, not just 'run it longer'.

scenarios.sample_answer: Flat is not proof of zero: p = 0.45 just means the data are consistent with no effect. Look at the confidence interval — if it excludes your MDE on both sides, you can reasonably kill it; if the interval is wide (underpowered), the test was inconclusive, so decide whether the idea merits a bigger or longer test. Ship only if the CI rules out meaningful harm and there is product rationale.
scenarios.scenario: The experiment ends flat: +0.2% lift, p = 0.45. The team concludes 'the feature does nothing' and wants to kill it.
scenarios.title: Interpreting a flat result
